My understanding of the question was that you wanted us to provide some information about how other jurisdictions in Canada fund land for new schools.
We were able to have a quick look at how they do it in British Columbia, Alberta, Manitoba, and Ontario.
It is not uncommon that new development provides funding for the acquisition of new school sites.
In British Columbia they have a school site's acquisition charge that is a charge for residential dwelling unit, which is collected at the subdivision or building permit stage.
The money is collected by the local government and provided to the school board for the acquisition of sites for new schools.
In Manitoba under provincial planning legislation.
Developers are required to dedicate up to 10% of land being subdivided for school purposes and a separate up to 10% for public reserve purposes.
And in Ontario, school boards can elect to impose education development charges under the Education Act, which are collected by the municipality on behalf of the school board.
These funds are used to fund the acquisition of school sites to accommodate growth related pupil needs.
They are again collected at the building permit stage on both residential and non-residential buildings.
Alberta is less clear and will require some more investigation.
School boards and cities are required to have joint planning agreements and there is some dedication of land required on subdivision by developers under the Municipal Government Act.
However, it will require more analysis to determine exactly how new school sites are funded.

School land purchases are not included full stop.

Schools are funded and built by the province not the city.

Furthermore beyond affordability these levees also raise fundamental issues of fairness.
Schools benefit everyone current homeowners, renters, future residents and even those in surrounding communities.
Yet the financial burden of these levees falls solely on buyers of new homes.
This approach is both incredibly inequitable and unsustainable.
